intro.title: Four registers, nothing new
intro.body:
This is the last unit of the course, and it teaches you no new Polish at all. Every phrase in it comes from one of the four registers C1 added: judging what something is like, talking about society and what a country owes its people, saying how sure you are, and choosing between formal and casual address.

Until now each of the four was practised on its own. Here they are mixed, because that is how they actually arrive — you form a view, you say how firmly you hold it, and you pitch it at the person in front of you.
intro.body_pl: Obiad jest gotowy. · Środowisko jest ważne. · Wydaje mi się… · Czy ma pan czas?

examples.en: It seems to me that the film is good. (hedging)
examples.pl: Wydaje mi się, że film jest dobry.

examples.en: Have you got time? — to a man you don't know. (register)

intro.title: Four registers, one shape each
intro.title_pl: …jest trudny · …jest ważne · Wydaje mi się… · Czy ma pan…?
intro.body:
Each register has a shape, and once the shape is visible you can hear which one someone is in.

Evaluation and society look identical on the page — a noun, jest, and an adjective — and differ only in what stands in the subject slot: a fridge and a deadline on one side, freedom and the law on the other. Hedging is the only one that does not describe anything: it wraps a sentence you have already built and lowers or raises how firmly you are claiming it. Register is the only one that changes the verb rather than the words.

That last row is what a capstone can show and no single unit could: the same fact goes out four different ways depending on who is listening.
intro.body_pl: Lodówka jest pusta. · Rząd ma nowy plan. · Tata pewnie jest w domu. · Czy ma pan czas?

rows: Wydaje mi się, że… / pewnie / naprawdę

intro.title: One conversation, four registers
intro.body:
Here is the whole thing chained together — you stop a stranger, you say how sure you are, you say what you think of a law, and you judge how the day is going. Nothing in it is new. Every sentence is a phrase from one of the four units you have already finished.

Read it once as a conversation before you start the exercises. Then it is over: this is the last thing the course has to teach you.
intro.body_pl: Dzień dobry. Czy ma pan czas? Wydaje mi się, że nowe prawo jest dobre. Szczerze mówiąc, ta praca jest trudna. Przynajmniej pogoda jest ładna.

quiz.prompt: You open the fridge and there is nothing in it. You say:
quiz.explain: pusty and pełny are the pair, and they are the two that answer this question. gotowa would say the fridge itself had been prepared, which is not a thing anyone says about a fridge.

quiz.prompt: You have finished cooking and lunch can go on the table. You say:
quiz.explain: gotowy is about the state of a thing, not about the person who made it — nothing in the sentence says who cooked. Obiad jest konieczny would be an argument for having lunch at all.

quiz.prompt: A deadline has been set that nobody could possibly meet. You say:
quiz.explain: The nie- on the front is the whole difference between the first two, and it is the only piece of the word that moves. Ten termin jest zwykły says the opposite — that there is nothing remarkable about it.

quiz.prompt: You are saying that clean air and nature matter. You say:
quiz.explain: Four subjects, one predicate. środowisko is the natural world; społeczeństwo is the people in it. Note the last one: technologia is feminine, so its adjective is ważna, not ważne.

quiz.prompt: The government has announced what it intends to do. You say:
quiz.explain: All four are things a government can have, and only the first is an intention. Rząd ma nowe prawo would mean the law has already been passed.

quiz.prompt: Someone asks what you make of technology, and you want to commit to a view rather than report a fact. You say:
quiz.explain: Myślę, że opens an opinion; Technologia jest nowa states something anyone could check. That is the difference between saying what you think and saying what is so.

quiz.prompt: You are fairly sure your father is home, but you have not checked. You say:
quiz.explain: pewnie lowers the claim to a guess. The bare sentence asserts it flatly, and naprawdę raises it further still — it insists. właściwie corrects something the other person said rather than hedging.

quiz.prompt: You want to offer your view of the film as an impression, not as a verdict. You say:
choices: Wydaje mi się, że film jest dobry.
quiz.answer: Wydaje mi się, że film jest dobry.
quiz.explain: Only the first lowers the claim. The other three go the other way — the bare statement asserts it, naprawdę insists on it, and Wiem, że claims you have grounds.

quiz.prompt: You are about to say something honest that the other person may not want to hear. You say:
choices: Szczerze mówiąc, ta praca jest trudna.
quiz.answer: Szczerze mówiąc, ta praca jest trudna.
quiz.explain: Szczerze mówiąc warns that candour is coming. Właściwie corrects, przynajmniej salvages one good thing from a bad situation, and całkiem softens the adjective itself — four different jobs on one sentence.

quiz.prompt: You stop a man you have never met and ask whether he has a moment. You say:
quiz.explain: Masz czas? is second person and is what you say to a friend. Czy masz pan czas? mixes the two — pan needs the third person ma, never masz. The last one is right in every respect except that he is a man.

quiz.prompt: You are at a café counter, ordering a coffee the way one does. You say:
quiz.explain: Chcę kawę is not rude, but it states a want where Polish expects a request. Masz kawę? asks whether the person has any, which is a different question altogether.

quiz.prompt: You greet a woman you have never met before. You say:
quiz.explain: Cześć is a real greeting, but only to somebody you are already on ty terms with — to a stranger it is not warm, it is presumptuous. The last two are goodbyes, and the wrong end of the conversation.

type_items.prompt_en: Have you got time? — to a man you don't know.
type_items.explain: The verb has already gone into the third person — ma, not masz — and pan is the word that put it there.
type_items.note: c1_register's own frame and blank, copied exactly rather than chosen afresh (capstone consistency rule, repair queue third run).

type_items.explain: obiad is masculine, so the adjective ends in -y. Nothing in the sentence says who did the cooking — gotowy describes the state the meal is in.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed (noun + jest + adjective), so a cloze at three words. Blanks c1_evaluation's teaching point.

type_items.explain: lodówka is feminine, so pusty becomes pusta. The ending is chosen by the fridge, not by the emptiness.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. Blanks c1_evaluation's teaching point.

type_items.explain: One word carries both halves: nie- on the front negates, and the -y agrees with termin. Polish writes it as a single word, not as two.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. Blanks c1_evaluation's teaching point.

type_items.explain: środowisko is neuter, which is why the adjective ends in -e here and in -a after wolność.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. ważne is one of c1_society's own taught forms, so the blank is on that pack's teaching point.

type_items.explain: This is the law, not the direction. You have known prawo since A1 inside na prawo — to the right — and it is the same string doing an entirely different job.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. Blanks c1_society's teaching point, and it is the pack's homograph — named in the explain rather than left to sting.

type_items.explain: problem is masculine and not alive, so the accusative after ma leaves it exactly as it stands.
type_items.note: FALLBACK CLAUSE, logged: this blank is NOT on the unit's teaching point. społeczeństwo is the register's own word, but blanking it would need a frame opening with the blank, and the environment item above already carries the society noun in its frame — two frame-initial blanks in one stage was the worse trade. The teaching point stays visible and is read whole.

type_items.explain: pewnie sits between the subject and the verb and changes nothing around it — the sentence underneath is the same one you have said since A1.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. Blanks c1_nuance's teaching point.

type_items.explain: naprawdę stands in front of the adjective and raises the claim. It never changes shape, whatever it is standing in front of.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. Blanks c1_nuance's teaching point.

type_items.prompt_en: I don't know exactly where the bank is.
type_items.explain: dokładnie narrows what you are denying: not that you have no idea, but that you cannot be precise about it.
type_items.note: Pisanie hard cap. Composed, cloze. Blanks c1_nuance's teaching point.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: I think the environment is important.
use_items.explain: The opinion frame takes the society sentence whole — nothing inside it changes, że just joins it on.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: It seems to me that this deadline is impossible.
use_items.answer: Wydaje mi się, że ten termin jest niemożliwy.
accepts: Wydaje mi się, że ten termin jest niemożliwy.
Wydaje mi się, że ten termin jest niemożliwy
use_items.explain: Hedging in front, evaluation behind. The hedge does not touch the sentence it is lowering.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Frankly speaking, this coffee is really good.
use_items.answer: Szczerze mówiąc, ta kawa jest naprawdę dobra.
accepts: Szczerze mówiąc, ta kawa jest naprawdę dobra.
Szczerze mówiąc, ta kawa jest naprawdę dobra
use_items.explain: Two hedging words in one sentence pulling opposite ways: szczerze mówiąc warns you are being blunt, naprawdę makes the praise stronger.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: The government has a new plan, but this plan is strange.
use_items.answer: Rząd ma nowy plan, ale ten plan jest dziwny.
accepts: Rząd ma nowy plan, ale ten plan jest dziwny.
Rząd ma nowy plan, ale ten plan jest dziwny
use_items.explain: Society on one side of ale, evaluation on the other. That is the whole capstone in one sentence.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Excuse me, could you help me? — to a man you don't know.
use_items.answer: Przepraszam, czy mógłby pan mi pomóc?
accepts: Przepraszam, czy mógłby pan mi pomóc?
Przepraszam, czy mógłby pan mi pomóc

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Mum is probably at home, and lunch is ready.
use_items.answer: Mama pewnie jest w domu, a obiad jest gotowy.
accepts: Mama pewnie jest w domu, a obiad jest gotowy.
Mama pewnie jest w domu, a obiad jest gotowy
use_items.explain: a joins two sentences that sit side by side without arguing with each other — ale would suggest the second undercuts the first.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: I don't know exactly what the government is doing.
use_items.answer: Nie wiem dokładnie, co robi rząd.
accepts: Nie wiem dokładnie, co robi rząd.
Nie wiem dokładnie, co robi rząd
use_items.explain: The subject stands after the verb inside the indirect question — co robi rząd, not co rząd robi. Both are heard; this is the ordinary one.

Type: Good morning. Could you help me? — to a woman you don't know.
use_items.answer: Dzień dobry. Czy mogłaby pani mi pomóc?
accepts: Dzień dobry. Czy mogłaby pani mi pomóc?
Dzień dobry. Czy mogłaby pani mi pomóc
Dzień dobry. Mogłaby pani mi pomóc?
Dzień dobry. Mogłaby pani mi pomóc
use_items.explain: The greeting and the request are pitched at the same person, so they have to agree — Cześć in front of this request would be a mismatch.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Dad said that the new law is good.
use_items.answer: Tata powiedział, że nowe prawo jest dobre.
accepts: Tata powiedział, że nowe prawo jest dobre.
Tata powiedział, że nowe prawo jest dobre
use_items.explain: Polish keeps the words he actually said, so jest stays in the present even though the English shifts it back.
